overview: Dacian communities lived around the Carpathians and lower Danube. Powerful rulers built mountain fortresses and sanctuaries before Roman conquest. This shared card separates those communities and kingdoms from the later Roman province. The map’s Dacians and Dacia snapshots are broad approximations, not exact historical borders.

periods.title: Burebista’s kingdom
periods.summary: Burebista brought a large kingdom together in the first century BCE. It fragmented after his death; Dacian political history did not follow one uninterrupted royal line.

periods.title: Kingdoms and mountain strongholds
periods.summary: Fortified centres, workshops and sanctuaries developed in the Orastie Mountains. Their best-known surviving works belong to the period before Roman conquest.

periods.title: A Roman province
periods.summary: After conquest in 106, part of the region became Roman Dacia. The province and its frontier lasted until the third-century withdrawal, conventionally dated to 271.

sections.title: A mountain capital built in layers

items.text: Sarmizegetusa Regia combined a fortress, a sacred area and civilian settlement. Builders cut artificial terraces into the hillside. More than a hundred terraces belonged to the civilian area, although only some have been excavated. Living in this capital meant adapting a mountain to human needs.

Paved paths and a monumental stairway connected parts of the sacred area. Round and rectangular shrines used stone and timber, while channels and cisterns helped manage water. The surviving foundations preserve impressive engineering, but do not tell us every detail of the ceremonies once held there.

sections.title: Dinner, clothes and keeping food for later

items.text: A study of seven Dacian sites in Transylvania found charred remains of cereals, legumes and fruits. These traces bring ordinary meals into view alongside famous battles. The evidence comes from particular excavated places; it cannot tell us what every Dacian household ate.

Burned seeds can survive long after a meal, basket or wooden house has disappeared. Archaeobotanists use such remains to investigate farming and food. A kitchen accident can leave a clue for someone many centuries later, although the original cook probably would not have appreciated that consolation.

A later research abstract identifies wheat, barley, rye and millet, together with broad beans, peas and lentils, at Late Iron Age sites in Transylvania. Flax and camelina also appear; the researcher connects these oil and fibre plants with production beyond food alone, including textiles.

Silos, clusters of charred grain and large ceramic containers provide evidence for storing supplies. Researchers interpret these finds as planning for food beyond the next meal. Storage mattered to households and larger centres alike: a harvest had to last much longer than the day it was gathered.

Excavators working at Sarmizegetusa in 1954 reported eight furnaces on a workshop terrace, along with ironworking evidence. Other finds included iron tools, painted pottery and glass vessels. The capital was a place where people made and used things, as well as a seat of political power.

The DACIT research project places the fortresses within a wider world of Mediterranean exchange and expanding iron metallurgy. Its archaeologists and engineers document ordinary objects as well as monuments. A digital model of a tool can help preserve evidence of skilled work that a king’s portrait would leave out.

sections.title: A real inscription, with an unsettled meaning

items.text: A large pottery vessel found in 1954 bears repeated stamps in Latin letters: “DECEBALVS PER SCORILO.” One proposed translation is “Decebalus made it through Scorilo.” Historian Dumitru Protase argued for this Latin reading; the extra idea of making is supplied in interpretation, not written as a separate word.

Other scholars interpreted the same stamps differently, including a reading that connected Decebalus and Scorilo as son and father. Protase disputed that explanation. This is an authentic ancient text, but its language and precise meaning remain debated. It is not a securely translated sample of everyday Dacian conversation.

sections.title: After conquest: Roman baths and public water

items.text: At the Roman city of Ulpia Traiana Sarmizegetusa, excavators found a run of 22 joined ceramic pipe sections near the financial procurator’s palace. The researcher interprets it as a bath water supply dating to around 170 CE. This evidence belongs to the Roman period, not the earlier mountain kingdom.

A loose ceramic tube does not automatically prove that a house had a bathroom or a sewer. The same study explains that tubes could also be used in building vaults. Archaeologists need to know where an object was found and how it connected to its surroundings before announcing ancient plumbing.

Two public fountains stood beside the Roman city’s forum in the Severan period, around the late second and early third centuries. A benefactor dedicated them in honour of the imperial family. Useful water, public generosity and religious display could share the same space; fetching water was part of city life.

ending.text: Roman conquest in 106 ended Decebalus’s kingdom. A Roman province followed in part of the region and lasted until the third century. These political changes did not mean that the population simply disappeared. The map’s Dacia endpoint of 200 is neither the conquest date nor the end of Roman rule.

sources.title: UNESCO: Dacian Fortresses of the Orastie Mountains
sources.note: Brief synthesis and criteria: six defensive works, religious and military architecture, first century BCE to first century CE. Does not validate imported borders.

sources.title: ICOMOS: Dacian Fortresses evaluation, 1999
sources.note: Dacia evaluation, PDF pages 143 to 146: Burebista, terraces, sanctuaries, workshops, water and 106 conquest. Avoids erroneous statements elsewhere about Herodotus and the location of the later Roman capital.

sources.title: Beatrice Ciuta: Archaeobotanical investigations on samples recovered from Dacian settlements located in Transylvanian area, 2023
sources.note: Accessible abstract only: charred plant remains from seven Transylvanian sites, cereals, legumes and fruits. Full article download was inaccessible.

sources.title: Beatrice Ciuta: Plants, Power, and Connectivity, conference abstract, 2025
sources.note: Printed pages 22 to 23, PDF pages 22 to 23: wheat, barley, rye, millet, pulses, flax and camelina; storage and textile interpretation. Conference abstract, not a full published excavation report.

sources.title: CIMEC: Excavations in the Orastie Mountains, 1949 to 1959
sources.note: Indexed institutional excavation history, 1954 account: furnace workshop, iron tools, painted pottery, glass and stamped vessel. Direct retrieval failed with an encoding error; indexed text was read.

sources.title: Technical University of Cluj-Napoca: DACIT heritage project
sources.note: Project description: Mediterranean commercial exchange, iron metallurgy, fortresses and three-dimensional documentation of everyday objects.

sources.title: Dumitru Protase: Decebalus per Scorilo, a new interpretation, 1986
sources.note: Thraco-Dacica VII, pages 146 to 153. Opening description and pages 152 to 153 discuss stamps, competing interpretations and the author’s proposed Latin reading. This interpretation is not presented as scholarly consensus.

sources.title: Gica Baestean: Ceramic water pipes in Colonia Dacica Sarmizegetusa, 1997 to 1998
sources.note: Sargetia XXVII/1, pages 253 to 260: 22 ceramic pipe sections at the procurator’s palace; suggested bath supply around 170; loose tubes also used in vault construction. This concerns Roman Ulpia Traiana Sarmizegetusa, not the mountain capital.

sources.title: Imola Boda: The Sacred Topography of Colonia Sarmizegetusa, 2015
sources.note: Acta Antiqua 55, pages 281 to 304, especially page 287: two Severan nymphaea beside the Trajanic forum, water supply and dedication by L. Ophonius Domitius Priscus.

sources.title: UNESCO: Frontiers of the Roman Empire, Dacia
sources.note: Property synthesis: Roman province and frontier from 106 to 271 CE, military and civilian settlements, extraction and exchange. Unrelated introductory dating claim is not used.
